The Grey heron Ardea cinerea is a large wading bird whose life history begins with incubation of its eggs. Eggs are maintained at a steady 36 °C [T = 36 °C] during the developmental period, and after approximately 25 days [ab = approximately 25 days] the altricial nestlings emerge. Newly hatched chicks have a wet body mass of just 35 grams [Wwb = 35 grams], reflecting the yolk-dependent provisioning within the calcareous egg. This modest starting mass is typical of many ardeids, which invest heavily in a small number of offspring per breeding attempt. Indeed, females typically lay between 3 and 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 5 eggs per clutch] and produce only a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year], a strategy that prioritizes parental investment per nestling over high fecundity. The relatively small brood size, combined with a prolonged incubation period, underscores the trade-off between egg production and the intensive biparental care required to raise semi-precocial chicks to independence.

Following hatching, the nestling phase is characterized by a period of rapid somatic growth and feather development. Under the thermal conditions typical of active metabolic periods in this species, which converge on approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], the young herons progress through a well-defined series of developmental milestones. A critical transition occurs when the downy chicks achieve sustained flight, an event known as fledging, which takes place roughly 52.5 days after hatching [tx = roughly 52.5 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This duration encompasses the time required for flight feather maturation and the achievement of sufficient wing loading to support aerial locomotion. The fledging period in Ardea cinerea is notably longer than in smaller ardeid species, a pattern that correlates with the larger ultimate body size attained by adults. During this extended nestling phase, both parents provision the developing chicks with fish and amphibians, ensuring that the energetic demands of feather growth and musculoskeletal development are met.

The juvenile period extends well beyond fledging, as young Grey herons gradually acquire the skills necessary for independent foraging. Sexual maturity is attained considerably later than the achievement of flight, marking a distinct life-stage transition. At a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], which represents the typical core temperature of an active, free-ranging individual, puberty occurs at an estimated 157.5 days after hatching [tp = 157.5 days after hatching]. This rather protracted juvenile phase likely reflects the time needed for individuals to develop proficient hunting techniques and accumulate sufficient body condition to support the metabolic costs of gonadal development. The delay between fledging and sexual maturity is a common pattern among large, long-lived waterbirds and is generally interpreted as a period of learning and somatic consolidation during which young birds refine their foraging efficiency and establish the territory holdings that will eventually support reproductive effort.

First breeding is deferred for an extended period after an individual reaches sexual maturity. The time since birth at first successful brood, measured under conditions approximating a body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], is approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching]. This represents a significant lag between the onset of physiological capacity for reproduction and its actual expression in the population. Several ecological factors likely contribute to this delay, including the necessity of securing a high-quality nesting territory in densely populated heronries, the energetic demands of constructing and defending a nest structure, and the need to accumulate sufficient endogenous reserves to sustain the demanding incubation and provisioning period. Across their extensive Palearctic range, first-year breeders are rarely observed, with most individuals entering the breeding population only in their second or third calendar year.

Adult Grey herons are relatively long-lived birds, and records from ringing programs have documented a maximum lifespan of approximately 37.5 years [am = approximately 37.5 years] under natural field conditions, with this value again referenced to the typical active body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. Such longevity is consistent with the slow life-history pace predicted by the species' relatively large adult body mass. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 1443 grams [Wwi = approximately 1443 grams], although there is considerable geographic variation across the species' wide distribution, ranging from about 1.02 to 2.08 kilograms [Wwi = about 1.02 to 2.08 kilograms] depending on sex and local food availability. This substantial adult mass is supported by a diet dominated by fish, amphibians, and aquatic invertebrates captured in shallow wetlands. The combination of deferred maturity, modest annual fecundity, and extended lifespan positions Ardea cinerea firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum for Ciconiiformes.
